questions.q: WHO IS ELIGIBLE TO VOTE BY MAIL?
questions.a:
To qualify to vote-by-mail, you must be:

- Absent from your county of residence on Election Day and during the early voting period,
- Sick or have a disability that prevents you from voting in person without assistance,
- 65 years old or older,
- Confined to jail serving a misdemeanor sentence; or confined to jail without bail pending trial for a felony or appeal of a felony conviction,
- Expecting to give birth within three weeks before or after Election Day, or
- Civilly committed under Chapter 841 of the Texas Health and Safety Code (https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/HS/htm/HS.841.htm)

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST A BALLOT BY MAIL?
questions.a: You may request a mail ballot application from your Early Voting Clerk (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) in the county where you are registered or use this application form (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1sa2b3wAH1Lep_jHHIJPBLjs2nRzz8C52/view). Read the application instructions carefully, complete the application, and return it to your Early Voting Clerk.

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE TO REQUEST A BALLOT BY MAIL?
questions.a: The last day to request a ballot (https://bbm.sos.state.tx.us/bbm.asp) by mail (https://webservices.sos.state.tx.us/forms/5-15f.pdf) is 11 days before the election. You can return your mail ballot request form through the mail or in-person to your county’s Early Voting Clerk (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: WHAT IS THE DEADLINE FOR SUBMITTING A BALLOT BY MAIL?
questions.a:
The Early Voting Clerk (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) must receive your marked ballot by 7:00 pm on Election Day if the carrier envelope is not postmarked (see below for exceptions).

- Ballots mailed within the United States (including military voters): Must be received by 5:00 pm the day after Election Day. The carrier envelope must be postmarked by 7:00 pm on Election Day.
- Ballots mailed from outside the United States (including military voters): Must be received by the fifth day after Election Day. The carrier envelope must be postmarked by 7:00 pm on Election Day.

Click here (https://www.votetexas.gov/voting-by-mail/carrier-envelope.html) for additional details.

questions.q: WHEN ARE MAIL BALLOTS MAILED OUT TO VOTERS WHO HAVE REQUESTED THEM?
questions.a: Ballots are mailed out 30 to 45 days before an election or 7 days after the county election office receives an application.

questions.q: HOW DO I COMPLETE MY MAIL BALLOT?
questions.a:
When you receive your ballot, be sure to:

1. Mark your ballot using a black or blue pen,
2. Place your ballot in the ballot envelope and seal it,
3. Place the ballot envelope in the carrier envelope,
4. Complete all information UNDER THE FLAP of the carrier-envelope, including your contact information, your voter ID number, AND the last four digits of your social security number,
5. Seal it, and
6. Sign your name OVER THE FLAP of the carrier envelope.

The Early Voting Clerk  (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)must receive your marked ballot by 7pm on Election Day or by the 5th day after Election Day if your ballot is submitted from outside of the United States.

questions.q: HOW DO I RETURN MY MAIL BALLOT IN PERSON?
questions.a: You can return your marked ballot in the official carrier envelope to the Early Voting Clerk on Election Day while the polls are open. You must show your ID and sign a form to return it in person. Contact your county election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: CAN I TRACK MY MAILED BALLOT AND/OR BALLOT BY MAIL APPLICATION?
questions.a: You can track the status of your ballot by mail application or ballot online here (https://teamrv-mvp.sos.texas.gov/BallotTrackerApp/#/login). If you have any issues with your state’s online tracker, please contact your local elections official (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: WHAT IF I REQUESTED A BALLOT BY MAIL BUT WANT TO VOTE IN PERSON?
questions.a: Bring your mail ballot and the pre-addressed outer return envelope to your polling place to be voided. If you don’t have your ballot or never received it, you will be able to cast a provisional ballot, and your vote will be counted once the county determines it never received a mail ballot from you.

questions.q: HOW DO I REQUEST A BALLOT BY MAIL AS AN OVERSEAS OR U.S. MILITARY VOTER?
questions.a:
Overseas citizens and U.S. military personnel can find information on how to register to vote and request a mail ballot at the Overseas Vote Foundation. (https://www.overseasvotefoundation.org/vote/home.htm)

For more information about Military and Overseas Voters, please visit your state's resource page.  (https://www.votetexas.gov/voting-by-mail/military-and-overseas-voters.html)

  Request your Ballot  (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/VoterInformation.htm)

questions.q: Does Texas allow ballot curing?
questions.a: Yes, Texas allows you to cure your absentee/mail ballot

questions.q: How do I cure my absentee/mail ballot?
questions.a: The deadline to cure your absentee/mail ballot by mail is by the 6th day after Election Day. The county will notify you if there is an issue with your absentee/mail ballot with instructions on how to cure your ballot.

questions.q: How do I track the status of my mail ballot?
questions.a: Track the status of your mail ballot using your state’s online tool (https://teamrv-mvp.sos.texas.gov/BallotTrackerApp/#/login).

questions.q: How do I cure my provisional ballot?
questions.a: If you voted a provisional ballot because you did not show a valid photo ID at the polls, you have until the 6th day after Election Day to provide evidence supporting your voting eligibility.

questions.q: What is a ballot drop box?
questions.a: A drop box is a secure, locked structure operated by election officials where voters can deliver their absentee ballot any time, day or night.

questions.q: Are drop boxes available in my state?
questions.a: No, drop boxes are not available in Texas.

questions.q: Where can I find ballot drop box locations?
questions.a:
To submit an absentee ballot in person, voters can hand-deliver their ballot to their county election official on Election Day only. Voters must show their ID and sign a form.

Please contact your county election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: Can I vote before Election Day in Texas?
questions.a: Yes. In Texas, you can vote before Election Day by voting early in person or by voting by mail if you qualify.

questions.q: Do I have to apply to vote early in Texas?
questions.a: No application is required to vote early in person. If you qualify to vote by mail, you must apply for a mail ballot. Learn more about voting by mail in Texas here. (https://www.vote411.org/texas#absentee-ballot-process)

questions.q: Where can I vote early in person in Texas?
questions.a: During the early voting period, you may be able to vote at any early voting location in your county. Contact your county elections office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for early voting locations and hours.

questions.q: How can I receive an early ballot in the mail?
questions.a: You must qualify and apply for a mail ballot. Learn more about the requirements for voting by mail in Texas here. (https://www.vote411.org/texas#absentee-ballot-process)

questions.q: Do I need an ID to vote early in Texas?
questions.a:
Yes. If you vote early in person, you must show an acceptable photo ID. If you vote by mail, you must provide identification information on your mail ballot application and ballot envelope. Read more about voter ID requirements in Texas here. (https://www.vote411.org/texas#voter-id-requirements)

Limited Ballots

A limited ballot is available during early voting for a registered voter who has moved from one Texas county to another and will not be registered in the new county before Election Day. A person may vote a limited ballot in person only at the main early voting location. Voters should contact their county election office (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for details.

questions.q: Who is eligible to vote in Texas?
questions.a:
You are eligible to register to vote in Texas if:

- A US citizen
- A resident of the county in which you intend to vote (See below for information if you have recently moved)
- At least 18 years old (you may register at 17 years and 10 months)
- Not convicted of a felony (unless your sentence is completed, including any probation or parole)
- Not declared mentally incompetent by a court of law
- Be registered 30 days before the election in which you plan to vote

questions.q: What if I have recently moved?
questions.a:
If you are already registered to vote in Texas and have moved or changed your name, you may update your voter registration online (http://www.texasonline.state.tx.us/NASApp/sos/SOSACManager).

You will need to have the following information to update your voter registration online:

- Current Texas Driver's License or Texas ID Card
- Social Security Number
- Voter Registration Card VUID (Voter Unique Identifier). The VUID is on your voter registration card, or you can find it by checking your voter registration status here (https://teamrv-mvp.sos.texas.gov/MVP/mvp.do)

If you live in the same county and missed the voter registration deadline, you may return to your old precinct to vote, but you will be required to complete a statement of residence confirming your new address in your new precinct.

questions.q: Can I vote in Texas if I have a felony conviction?
questions.a: In Texas, you lose your voting rights if you are convicted of a felony. Once someone has "fully discharged" their sentence, including court-ordered supervision, probation, or parole, their right to vote is automatically restored. Pretrial detention and misdemeanor convictions do not restrict your voting rights in Texas.

questions.q: How do I vote in Texas if I don’t have a permanent address?
questions.a: It is not mandatory for citizens to possess a "permanent home" for voter registration. A citizen can provide an alternative description of their residence, even if they are experiencing homelessness, as long as it enables the authorities to identify and assign a voting precinct to them. This precinct assignment ensures that the voter receives the appropriate ballot. The mailing address on their registration form can be a P.O. box, local shelter, advocacy organization, outreach center, or the home of someone who will accept mail for them.

questions.q: Can students vote in Texas?
questions.a: Yes. Students may register and vote in Texas if they meet the state's voter eligibility requirements. Students can register using either their school address or their home address, but they may only be registered and vote in one location.

questions.q: Do I need an ID to register to vote in Texas?
questions.a: To register to vote in Texas, you must include your state driver's license number or personal ID number issued by the State Department of Public Safety on the application form (https://webservices.sos.state.tx.us/vrapp/index.asp).

questions.q: What types of ID are accepted for registration?
questions.a: See above.

questions.q: What if I don’t have an ID?
questions.a:
If you do not have either of these numbers, you may provide the last four digits of your social security number on the form. If you don't have a social security number you must check the box stating you do not have this information.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: When are official election results available in Texas?
questions.a: Official results are never available on Election Day. Election officials are working around the clock to count a large number of ballots, and it’s essential that they take the time to make sure every vote is counted.

questions.q: Where can I find official election results?
questions.a:
Official election results will be uploaded on Texas’ Secretary of State website (https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/historical/index.shtml) as they become available.

  Official Results  (https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/historical/index.shtml)

questions.q: What does a poll worker do in Texas?
questions.a: Poll workers, called election workers in Texas, typically help run elections by checking in voters, issuing ballots, assisting voters, operating voting equipment, and helping open and close polling locations.

questions.q: What qualifications do I need to be a poll worker in Texas?
questions.a:
To be an election worker in Texas you must:

- Be a qualified voter in the county where you serve
- Complete any required training
- Not be a candidate for public office in the election
- Not be related within certain degrees to a candidate, the county election officer, or the county voter registrar

Texas also allows eligible high school students to serve as student election clerks if they meet program requirements.

questions.q: Are poll workers paid in Texas?
questions.a: Yes. Election workers are paid for their service. Compensation may vary by location and position. Contact your local elections official (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for more information.

questions.q: How do I apply to be a poll worker in Texas?
questions.a: You can apply by contacting your county election office or county clerk. (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm)

questions.q: What is a provisional ballot?
questions.a: Provisional ballots ensure that all voters can cast a ballot even if voter eligibility isn’t certain when they vote. Voters can mark a provisional ballot, and election workers set it aside until eligibility is verified at a later time.

questions.q: Does Texas offer provisional voting?
questions.a: Yes, Texas offers provisional voting if you meet specific conditions.

questions.q: How do I vote a provisional ballot?
questions.a:
You are eligible to vote a provisional ballot if:

- You claim to be an eligible voter, but your name does not appear on the list of registered voters, and your registration cannot be determined by the voter registrar.
- You’ve applied for a ballot by mail but haven’t returned it or canceled it.
- You vote during extended polling hours ordered by a state or federal court.
- You don't present any acceptable form of identification.

If you claim to be registered, but your name is not on the list of registered voters, the presiding election judge will call the voter registrar to determine if you are registered. If registration can be confirmed and you can show identification, you may vote a regular ballot or be directed to the correct precinct if you are in the wrong precinct.

questions.q: How do I cure my provisional ballot?
questions.a: If you vote a provisional ballot, be sure to bring your acceptable form of ID to your local voter registrar’s office within 6 calendar days after the election so that your provisional ballot is counted.

questions.q: How do I confirm that my provisional ballot was counted?
questions.a: Provisional voters will receive a notice in the mail by the 10th day after the election letting them know if their provisional ballots were counted and if they were not counted, the reasons why.

questions.q: WHAT IF I NEED A HELPER TO VOTE IN-PERSON?
questions.a:
If you vote in person, the notice of voting order  (https://elections.mctx.org/pdf/RUN052422/Notice%20of%20Voting%20Order%20Priority%20for%20Voters%20with%20Certain%20Disabilities.pdf)allows a voter with a disability and their helper to request to move ahead of other voters in line.

Persons who assist voters with an absentee ballot application, absentee ballot, or an in-person ballot must provide their relationship to the voter and address. For the absentee and in-person ballot, the person who assists must sign an oath and mark that they did not receive compensation.

questions.q: WHAT IF I AM PHYSICALLY UNABLE TO MARK MY BALLOT?
questions.a:
If you are physically unable to mark your ballot or cannot read the ballot, you are eligible for assistance.

- You may choose anyone as an assistant except your employer, an officer of your union, or an agent of either.
- The assistant must take an oath of assistance administered by an election official.
- The assistant may read the ballot to you and mark your ballot.*
- If you do not choose your own assistant, two election officials (of different political parties in the General Election) may assist you.
- Poll watchers and inspectors can observe the assistance by election officials.

*New Texas laws have gone into effect that may affect voter assistance. Please contact your county election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm) for the most up–to-date information.

questions.q: WHAT IF I NEED AN INTERPRETER?
questions.a: An interpreter may be used if you and the election official cannot speak the same language. The interpreter must be a registered voter of the county, must take the oath of assistance at the polls, and may interpret for any number of voters.

questions.q: WHAT IF I HAVE VISUAL DISABILITIES?
questions.a: All Texas counties must provide one direct electronic voting machine (DRE) at each polling place for voters with visual disabilities so that they may cast their ballot without assistance. These machines are equipped with headphones and a keypad.

questions.q: WHAT OTHER RESOURCES ARE THERE FOR VOTERS WITH DISABILITIES?
questions.a:
To find out more about how you may receive support while voting, click here. (http://www.votetexas.gov/voters-with-special-needs/)

For more information, you can utilize the American Association of People With Disabilities (AAPD) (http://www.aapd.com/what-we-do/voting/) resource.

If you are a person with a disability and have questions about your voting rights, call Disability Rights Texas’ Voting Hotline at 1-888-796-VOTE (8683)

questions.q: WHAT IF I MISSED THE VOTER REGISTRATION DEADLINE AFTER I MOVED?
questions.a:
If you live in the same county and missed the voter registration deadline, you may return to your old precinct to vote, but you will be required to complete a statement of residence confirming your new address in your new precinct. Many Texas counties have county-wide voting, so voters can vote at any precinct within their county.

If you moved to a new county and missed the voter registration deadline, you may be eligible to vote a limited ballot at your county’s main voting location during the early voting period. The limited ballot application will also act as a voter registration application. You may NOT vote a limited ballot on Election Day.

For more information on updating your voter registration, click here (http://www.votetexas.gov/register-to-vote/did-you-change-something) or contact your county election officials (https://absentee.vote411.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm).

questions.q: WHAT DO I NEED TO REGISTER TO VOTE?
questions.a:
Here is what you need to know to register in Texas:

- On the application form, you must include your state driver's license number or personal ID number issued by the State Department of Public Safety.
- If you do not have either of these numbers, you may provide the last four digits of your social security number on the form.
- If you don't have a social security number, you must check the box stating you do not have this information.
- All voters must present an acceptable form of photo ID to vote at the polls. A list of acceptable forms of photo ID can be found here. (https://www.vote411.org/texas#id-needed-for-voting)
- A student ID is not a form of valid voter ID.

Use our online tool (https://www.vote411.org/register) to register to vote today!

questions.q: Does Texas require employers to give time off to vote?
questions.a: Yes. Texas employers must provide paid time off to vote on Election Day if you do not have at least two consecutive hours available to vote outside of your work schedule. Contact your employer about your voting options before Election Day.

questions.q: CAN I USE MY STUDENT ID TO VOTE?
questions.a: No, a student ID is not a form of valid voter ID.

questions.q: WHAT IF I DON’T HAVE A PHOTO ID?
questions.a:
Registered voters without photo ID, who cannot reasonably obtain one, may sign a form and present the original or a copy of one of the following documents with the voter’s name and address to vote a regular ballot:

- Voter registration card
- Certified birth certificate
- Current utility bill
- Bank statement
- Government check
- Paycheck
- Any other government document, such as an out-of-state driver’s license or expired Texas driver’s license

questions.q: CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THE FORM I NEED TO FILL OUT IF I DON’T HAVE A PHOTO ID?
questions.a:
The form is called a “Voter’s Declaration of Reasonable Impediment or Difficulty.” The voter must mark on the form one of the following reasons for not providing a photo ID.*

- Lack of transportation
- Disability or illness
- Lack of birth certificate or other documents needed to obtain an acceptable form of photo ID
- Work schedule
- Family responsibilities
- Lost or stolen identification
- Acceptable form of photo ID applied for but not received

*ID address does not have to match the voter registration address.

Once you sign the form and show your ID you will be able to cast a normal ballot at your polling place.

The name on your photo ID and the list of registered voters must match. If your name is substantially similar*, you may still be able to vote a normal ballot; however, you must also submit an affidavit stating that you are the same person as is listed on the list of registered voters.

If you do not have any of these forms of ID, you can get an Election Identification Certificate to present at the polling place. To find out more about these certificates, click here. (http://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/electionID.htm)

*“Substantially similar” means if your name is slightly different, is a common variation of your formal name, contains an initial, middle name or former last name or your first, middle or last name is in a different field on the ID than on the list of registered voters.

Voters can call or text 844-338-8743 at any time to reach VoteRiders Voter ID Helpline

questions.q: What is the deadline to register to vote in Texas?
questions.a:
- Online registration deadline: Not available
- Register by mail deadline: Postmarked 30 days before Election Day
- In-person registration deadline: 30 days before Election Day

questions.q: How can I register to vote in Texas?
questions.a:
- In-person. Visit your county’s voter registrar office (https://www.sos.texas.gov/elections/voter/votregduties.shtml).
- By mail. Pick up a voter registration application from your county’s Voter Registrar office (https://www.sos.texas.gov/elections/voter/votregduties.shtml), public libraries (https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/laws/texas-public-libraries.shtml), government offices (https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/laws/voter-registration-agencies.shtml), or high schools.
- Online. Fill out your voter registration application through Texas’ online portal (https://vrapp.sos.state.tx.us/index.asp), then print, sign, and mail it to your county’s voter registrar office (https://www.sos.texas.gov/elections/voter/votregduties.shtml).

questions.q: How do I check my voter registration?
questions.a: Check your voter registration status at Am I Registered?  (https://teamrv-mvp.sos.texas.gov/MVP/mvp.do)or with your county voter registrar.  (https://www.sos.texas.gov/elections/voter/votregduties.shtml)

questions.q: Does Texas have online voter registration?
questions.a: No, Texas does not have online voter registration available.

questions.q: Is same-day voter registration available in Texas?
questions.a: No, Texas does not have same-day voter registration.

questions.q: Can I pre-register to vote?
questions.a: Yes, you can pre-register at 17 years and 10 months if you’ll be 18 years old by Election Day.

questions.q: Who is eligible to register in Texas?
questions.a: Check if you’re eligible to register here (https://www.vote411.org/texas#eligibility-requirements).

questions.q: WHAT IS OPTICAL SCAN VOTING?
questions.a:
With optical scan voting, you will receive a card or sheet of paper, which you take over to a private table or booth. The card has the names of the various candidates and ballot measures printed on it.

- With a pen or pencil, you fill in a little box, circle, or space between two arrows.
- When you are finished filling out all the cards, you may bring the cards over to a ballot box, where poll workers will show you how to put the cards in the box.
- Or in some places, you may feed the completed cards or papers into a computer device that checks your card or paper right there at the polling place to make sure you have voted the way you want to and counts the votes.

questions.q: WHAT IS DIRECT RECORDING ELECTRONIC VOTING?
questions.a:
Direct Recording Electronic (DRE) is the newest system in use in the U.S. All the information about who and what you are voting for is on an electronic screen like a TV or computer screen.

There are many variations of DREs because many companies are inventing new ones, and many cities, counties, and states are trying them out.

- Usually, after you have signed in, the poll workers will give you a card that you slide into a device to start your voting session.
- Some of these devices will show all candidates and ballot choices on one big screen. Often, with these big screen devices you push a button next to the name of the candidate you want to vote for (or yes or no on a ballot measure).
- On other DREs, the screen is set up to show pages. There will probably be one thing on which to vote on each screen or page. For example, on one screen or page, you might vote for the president. Then you might move to the next page to vote for a senator. Often these small-screen devices have a touch screen, where you touch the screen next to the name of the person you want to vote for.
- Other devices have a keypad, and some have a keyboard, so you can write in the name of someone you want to vote for.
- You let the system know you are finished voting by pushing a button, touching the screen or entering something on a keypad.

questions.q: WHAT IS PAPER BALLOT VOTING?
questions.a:
Paper ballots are one of the oldest ways of voting in America. They are still used in a few places on Election Day.

- When you come to the polling place, you will get a paper ballot from the poll worker.
- You take it to the voting booth, and use a pen or pencil to mark a box next to your candidate and issue choices.
- You then drop the marked ballot into a sealed ballot box.

The following vendors are currently certified by the State of Texas: Election Systems & Software (ES&S) and Hart InterCivic (https://www.votetexas.gov/voting/voting-systems.html)

You can learn more about voting systems by checking out the Elections Assistance Commission's (EAC) resource. (https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/system-certification-process)
